catalog_quote: [p. 28] Maale has two tones, high and low; the former is represented in the following discussion by ('); low-tone is left unmarked. Tone is realized only on vowels, there are no syllabic nasals or other tone-bearing consonants. ... [p. 37] Since Ometo languages are known to have a tone-accent system or stress-accent system, the Maale case raises the question whether this language shows an innovation or retention of a tone system that is lost in the other Ometo languages. ... Maale is different from these languages because it allows sequences of low or high tones in a word, while in the former languages an underived word must have one and only one high tone-accent which is positionally restricted to the ultimate or penultimate vowel. Because of this, in simple lexical forms Maale allows more combinations of tone patterns than the other Ometo languages as shown in this chapter and in Azeb Amha (1997). ... With the exception of five words (three pronouns and two spatial expressions) the minimum independent word in Maale consists of two-syllables/tone bearing units. This combined with the fact that H tone has a limited distribution in word-final position may suggest that Maale perhaps shifted from a tone-accent system to a more classic tonal system.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Maale is a two-tone language (H vs L on every vowel; long vowels/diphthongs carry one tone). Tone is lexically contrastive and a word may carry any sequence of H and L (LL, LH, HL, HH, LLL, HHL, LLH, HHH, LHL, HLL etc; HLH unattested in simple words; word-final H is comparatively rare). No word stress is described and the term 'stress' is never applied to Maale; the grammar explicitly says Maale is NOT a tone-accent/stress-accent system of the Ometo type (one culminative H restricted to the ultimate or penultimate vowel, as in Gofa, Wolaitta, Gamo, Zayse) but a 'more classic tonal system'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable / not mentioned (no stress described).
new_statements.exceptions: Minimum independent word is disyllabic except five monosyllables (short pronouns ta, ne, nu and locatives ?óó 'up', luu 'down', sóó 'sideways' are listed, p. 28; 'five words' p. 37). Tonal irregularity of waari 'goat' (plural waaró HHH instead of expected LLH, p. 37). Some morphemes have fixed tone (-ó, -e-), others copy the preceding tone (-atsi) or optionally receive H (infinitive -itsi after L roots); a productive H-insertion rule places H on the last vowel of an all-L stem before copula -ke, instrumental -na, ablative -ppa (pp. 34-35).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone described on citation forms of nouns/adjectives/adverbs and on verb roots (bound; cited with inflection). Phrase level (§2.5.4, pp. 35-36): downdrift in HLHL sequences; 'There do not appear to be tone rules cutting across word boundaries' — modifiers and heads keep their own tones.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Maale (self-name; Glottolog 'Male (Ethiopia)', male1284, ISO mdy) from fieldwork with native speakers in the Maale area of South Omo; no dialect split is invoked. Amha 2001: 3 flags that Hirut 1988's data may partly be Gofa (gofa1235), so that thesis should not be taken as Maale without checking.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.5 Tone (pp. 28-37): Maale has two lexically contrastive tones H and L on vowels; multiple H or L per word allowed (LL, LH, HL, HH, LLL, HHL, LLH, HHH.; HLH unattested in simple words); p. 37 explicitly contrasts Maale with the tone-accent/stress-accent systems of other Ometo languages (one culminative H on ultimate or penultimate vowel) and calls Maale a 'more classic tonal system'. The word 'stress' is never applied to Maale itself; no word-stress rule is given.
